name: Kele
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Carrington, John F. 1949. A comparative study of some Central African gong-languages. Mémoires de l'Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Section des Sciences morales et politiques, T. XVIII fasc. 3. Brussels: IRCB. (KAOW-ARSOM digitised memoir; saved)
catalog_locator: p. 45, chapter V 'The nature of the signals', subsection b) 'Rhythmic patterns'; continuation p. 46
catalog_quote: b) Rhythmic patterns. In addition to tonal variations between an essentially high and an essentially low tone, the syllables of a word in speech can show differences in prominence which give the word a characteristic rhythm. In Kele and some surrounding languages the most prominent syllable in the spoken language is the penultimate, irrespective of the grammatical nature of this syllable. On the other hand, in some other Central African languages, e.g. Ngala (cf. 32, p. 8) the most prominent syllable is the initial syllable of the radical. [p. 46] ... rhythm may be the only factor determinative of meaning in gong-language elements which have identical tonal patterns.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kele is a two-tone (H/L) language; independently of tone, word-level prominence (rhythmic stress) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word regardless of its morphological status (prefix, radical or suffix), unlike Ngala-type languages with radical-initial prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Carrington. (Stapleton 1903 p.4, with the opposite primary rule, puts a 'secondary and weaker accent' on the penult when more than two syllables follow the stem-initial syllable.)
new_statements.exceptions: Carrington gives none. Contradicting older source: Stapleton 1903 pp.4-5 states for 'the Congo languages' incl. Kele that the main accent is on the stem-initial syllable (nasal-only prefixes count with the stem syllable), with accent shift marking the Kele negative imperative/subjunctive (owangeke; sec. 563 p.184) and recent Swahili loans keeping penult accent -- a pre-tonal analysis that likely conflates tone with stress; Carrington, the tonologist of Kele, explicitly separates prominence from tone and says penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word in speech ('the syllables of a word in speech'); prominence described as rhythm, reproduced on the slit-gong by beat spacing rather than amplitude (p.46); Carrington notes rhythm alone distinguishes Kele gong-phrases with identical tone patterns (botandalakoko vs tolakondeloko).
new_statements.identity_note: Carrington's 'Kele' is the Lokele of the Yakusu (Yakoso) area on the Congo river below Kisangani (his Yawani dialect group), i.e. Glottolog kele1255 'Kele-Foma' proper; Stapleton 1903 likewise wrote from Yakusu. Motingea 2012 describes the Mbooso variety (Yawembe group, Lomame mouth) of the same language. Carrington 1977 'likile' is a different, neighbouring speech form and was not used.

sources.note: p.45 (section b 'Rhythmic patterns'): besides H/L tone, syllables differ in prominence; 'In Kele and some surrounding languages the most prominent syllable in the spoken language is the penultimate, irrespective of the grammatical nature of this syllable', contrasted with Ngala where prominence is radical-initial (citing Guthrie). p.46: rhythm (prominence) alone can distinguish gong-phrases with identical tonal patterns.

sources.note: pp.4-5 'B. On Accent' sec. 8: 'In the Congo languages the main accent falls on the initial syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables.. follow the accented syllable a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult'; 8(c) accent shifted for grammatical distinction in Kele owangeke; sec. 9 note: Swahili loans in Kele 'not yet brought under the rule of accent which obtains in Kele' and heard with penult accent; sec. 563 p.184: Kele negates the subjunctive 'by shifting the stress from the first syllable of the stem to the first syllable containing the Subjunctive sign'. Pre-tonal mission…
